editorNote: The weekly record of games, home computers and digital culture.
morningLine: Ghostbusters takes the holiday spotlight; the modem opens a door to games, neighbors and shopping.

lead.headline: Ghostbusters leads Activision’s million-dollar holiday comeback bid
lead.dek: Activision plans more than $1 million in holiday advertising as computer software takes a larger place in its business.
body: Activision is putting Ghostbusters at the center of a holiday comeback bid. In the November 3 Billboard, Faye Zuckerman reports an advertising budget exceeding $1 million for the selling season. President James Levy says shipments are picking up after a slow summer, with David Crane’s newly shipped Ghostbusters and Designer’s Pencil carrying the company’s hopes for fresh hits.

The planned push reaches beyond the software counter. Radio contests, television spots and a major print campaign are in the works. These are the company’s announced plans, not a tally of advertising already aired. A familiar movie name gives the game a ready-made calling card, but Activision still has to persuade households to buy software.

The recovery has a difficult starting point. The fiscal quarter ending June 30 brought a $3.6 million loss on $6.2 million in sales, figures recalled in this week’s report rather than new weekly earnings. Levy describes declining video-game orders alongside an increasingly apparent computer-software business.

That shift is also a change of identity. Levy expects the old video-game-company image to fade in about six months and insists that Activision is in the business for the long term. Ghostbusters is thus more than a seasonal attraction: it is a prominent test of the cartridge pioneer’s move toward the home-computer shelf.

stories.headline: The bulletin board becomes a neighborhood without borders
body: November’s COMPUTE! finds a growing neighborhood behind the telephone jack. Home-operated bulletin boards carry messages, public-domain software, classified advertisements and technical help. Most accept only one caller at a time, so the busy signal remains as familiar as the welcome screen.

Chicago programmer John Semenek recalls finding only one local Atari board and now reports at least 20 in the metropolitan area. Stan and Susie Subeck’s Valley Girl BBS adds adventure games and trivia to the conversation, with the children helping maintain the family system.

The volunteer labor is substantial. A survey by Plumb editor Ric Manning puts average setup expense above $3,000, another $50 in monthly running costs and maintenance or data entry at up to 50 hours a month. Kent Fillmore’s Apple II-based Draco-Net points toward a larger ambition: a proposed franchise in every area code, not yet a completed national network.

stories.headline: Shopping by modem: CompuServe’s Electronic Mall is open all night
body: The home computer is becoming a catalog counter. Selby Bateman’s November COMPUTE! report puts CompuServe above 130,000 subscribers and its Electronic Mall above 80 merchants. WaldenBooks, American Express, Commodore, McGraw-Hill, Microsoft and American Airlines are among the named participants.

The Mall keeps its doors open around the clock, with product descriptions, merchant-query mailboxes, shipping information and order forms. It is a text-heavy proposition for ordinary home computers, contrasting with graphical videotex systems that call for special equipment.

Price and equipment still separate the services. Viewtron requires a $600 AT&T Sceptre terminal. Chicago’s Keyfax is reported at $10–$15 a month plus a $40 software package, with home shopping still forthcoming. The shopping trip may avoid the street, but it does not avoid the telephone connection or the bill.

stories.headline: Commodore’s Plus/4 trades game features for built-in office tools
body: Commodore’s Plus/4 offers a different bargain from the game-oriented 64. October’s COMPUTE! report describes a $300, 64K machine with four applications in ROM: word processing, spreadsheet work, file management and business graphics. International Tri Micro developed the integrated 3-Plus-1 package.

BASIC 3.5 supplies more than 75 commands, and bank switching leaves roughly 60K available to BASIC. Graphics reach 320 by 200 with 128 hues, but hardware sprites are absent and two tone generators replace the C64’s more flexible SID sound system.

The trade-offs matter at the counter. Most VIC-20 and C64 software does not run unchanged; cassette and joystick connectors differ, although the 1541 drive and serial printers remain usable. The built-in word processor stops at 99 lines. This is an October preview for fall buyers, not confirmation of a launch during this week.

computerItems.title: Ghostbusters
computerItems.summary: Newly shipped title by David Crane is central to Activision’s holiday campaign; exact release day and price not established here.

computerItems.title: Archon II: ADEPT
computerItems.summary: October COMPUTE! reports Electronic Arts introduction: strategy plus action, spells and energy-point capture, human or computer opponent; Atari requires 48K, also Commodore 64; suggested retail $40. Not a verified release this week.

computerItems.title: Skyfox
computerItems.summary: Electronic Arts Apple II-family disk game: single-player aircraft-and-tank combat defending Federation asteroid bases, training and 15 scenarios; suggested retail $40. October report.

computerItems.title: Dragonriders of Pern
computerItems.summary: Shay Addams’s October review emphasizes diplomacy and alliances alongside Thread-fighting action. Epyx: disk C64/Atari, cassette C64; $39.95. Period review, not a new weekly release.

computerItems.title: KoalaPad for PCjr
computerItems.summary: November review requires PCjr with 128K, disk drive, DOS 2.1 and color display. Roughly 6×8-inch pad, 4-inch-square sensitive surface and 5½-foot cord to joystick port. KoalaPainter uses 160×200 with 16 colors; reviewer questions failure to use higher resolution. No price verified.

computerItems.title: Commodore Plus/4
computerItems.summary: 64K productivity-oriented machine, built-in 3-Plus-1, BASIC 3.5 and 128 hues; incompatible with most C64 software. Preliminary October report, not exact-week launch.

computerItems.title: Tel-A-Modem 212A
computerItems.summary: Code-A-Phone combines telephone and modem with two lines for simultaneous voice/data use. November modem survey; no verified model price.

softwareList.name: Designer’s Pencil
softwareList.detail: Activision hopes this newly shipped title will join Ghostbusters as a holiday hit; source does not establish specs or price.

softwareList.name: WizType
softwareList.detail: Sierra typing tutor using Wizard of Id characters, game/drill/practice modes and custom lessons. Atari version reviewed; Atari, C64 or Apple II-family with at least 32K and disk drive; $34.95.

softwareList.name: OmniWriter & OmniSpell
softwareList.detail: Human Engineered Software C64 package: 30,000-word spelling checker, 34,000-character files and linked printing; reviewer finds manual page-break handling troublesome. $59.95; requires disk drive and compatible printer.

market.headline: Activision bets on the computer shelf
market.summary: Levy reports video-game orders diminishing and computer-software orders becoming more apparent. More than $1 million in planned holiday advertising backs the shift; June-quarter losses remain the backdrop.

worldAnchor.headline: Indira Gandhi assassinated in New Delhi
worldAnchor.summary: India’s prime minister was shot and killed in New Delhi on October 31. An emergency cabinet meeting and heightened security followed.

bbsNote.headline: Atari adventures move onto the bulletin board
bbsNote.summary: November COMPUTE! documents live community systems, online games and falling modem prices. These are magazine-month observations, not dated posts or claims of a launch during the target week.

posts.text: Reported by Kathy Yakal: Stan and Susie Subeck offer adventure games and a trivia quiz to callers.
Kent Fillmore operates a home board and proposes a national franchise network with space for local user-group boards; the network remains a proposal.
Sharon Darling reports 300-bps models remain economical for local conversation while 1200-bps transfers reduce paid connection time; terminal software often costs extra.
Ric Manning’s survey, cited in COMPUTE!, reports average setup over $3,000, another $50 monthly and maintenance up to 50 hours monthly.

curiosity.headline: A Chicago Atari board speaks Valley Girl
curiosity.summary: The Subeck family turns Southern California slang into a BBS interface.
curiosity.detail: November COMPUTE! reports that Valley Girl BBS calls deleting a message “bag” and exiting “de-val.” A 13-year-old daughter’s Valspeak inspired the theme; the children also help maintain the system. These are period menu descriptions, not newly collected messages.
